analysis.one_liner: Funds passenger rail safety technology and bars further delays in installing anti-collision train controls.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Transportation Committee without ever receiving a hearing, vote, or floor action after its January 2018 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: Positive train control (PTC) is a GPS-based system that automatically slows or stops a train before a collision or derailment. Congress had required railroads to install it, but allowed the deadline to be pushed back repeatedly. This bill would have locked in the end-of-2018 deadline, banned any further extensions, given commuter and intercity passenger rail operators $2.572 billion in federal grants to install the technology, barred new passenger routes from opening without PTC in place, and required Amtrak to report its installation progress route by route.
analysis.who_benefits: Riders on commuter and intercity passenger trains, who would get the anti-collision technology installed sooner and more completely; and the passenger rail agencies and Amtrak, which would receive dedicated federal money to pay for it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Train riders and passenger rail operators

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any further extension of the legal deadline for railroads to have positive train control operating, beyond December 31, 2018. [S2] [S3]
Authorizes $2.572 billion in federal grants to help operators of regularly scheduled intercity and commuter passenger rail pay for PTC installation. [S2] [S3]
Bars passenger operators from starting service on any new route unless a PTC system is fully implemented and operational on that route. [S2] [S3]
Requires Amtrak to file detailed route-by-route status reports on PTC progress, covering the Northeast Corridor, long-distance routes, and state-supported routes. [S2] [S3]
Removes the option for railroads to submit an alternative, slower schedule for implementing PTC in their revised plans. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads, which would lose the ability to seek more time and would have to finish spending billions on PTC equipment on the existing timetable; and ultimately taxpayers, who fund the passenger-rail grants.

drawbacks.text: Freight railroads had spent heavily on PTC and warned that hard deadlines risked service disruptions if the technology was not ready; the bill offered them no relief on the freight-railroad side, only grants for passenger operators. [S2] [S3]

The grant authorization was oddly written: the $2.572 billion was authorized 'to remain available until December 31, 2018,' the same year the bill was introduced, leaving almost no time to appropriate or spend it. [S3]
By forbidding new passenger routes without operational PTC, the bill could delay planned new or expanded passenger service where installation lagged. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is real: positive train control prevents the kind of collisions and derailments that have killed passengers and crews, and Congress had already stretched the deadline once before. The cost falls mainly on freight railroads that were already legally required to build the system, and the bill pairs the hard deadline with money to help passenger operators comply, which softens the burden on the services riders actually use. The main design flaw is the grant window, which expires the same year the money would have to be spent — a drafting problem, not a reason to abandon the safety deadline.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its rail subcommittee, and no committee vote, hearing, or floor action ever happened before the two-year Congress ended. [S5] [S1]

narrative.text: Representative Peter DeFazio of Oregon, joined by 10 cosponsors (9 Democrats and 1 Republican), introduced the bill on January 11, 2018. [S1] [S4]
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure. [S5]
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, where it sat for the remainder of the 115th Congress. [S5]
The full action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote at any point. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Freight railroads, which kept the option of seeking further schedule relief on their multibillion-dollar PTC obligation, and passenger rail operators, who never received the dedicated grant money. Riders got neither the earlier deadline nor the funding.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lock in the end-of-2018 positive train control deadline and fund passenger rail installation.

for.name: 10 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day of introduction.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee for a markup or vote; it stayed at subcommittee referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: Freight railroad industry
against.role: Freight rail carriers facing PTC compliance deadlines
against.what_they_did: Publicly sought repeated extensions of the PTC deadline and pushed back against hard completion dates in the period around this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was nearly all Democrats (9 of 10), with a single Republican, and the committee chair who declined to act was a Republican; there was no recorded vote to measure the split. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would have stripped railroads' ability to submit alternative schedules or win further deadline extensions, forcing completion of their multibillion-dollar PTC obligation on the existing timetable. Their interest in delay ran against the public's interest in the safety systems being finished. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Commuter and intercity passenger rail operators
industries.note: Operators would receive $2.572 billion in grants to pay for PTC, directly lowering the cost of compliance for services riders depend on. [S3]
Vendors of PTC equipment and integration services would gain a firm, unextendable mandate and new federal funding for passenger-rail installations. [S2] [S3]
